title: The daily banis
hook: Nitnem means daily practice: set prayers at dawn, at dusk and at night

segments.voice: Yesterday, your simran: a time, a place and a length that fit your real life. Your line was your five minutes. And if a day slips, there's always coming back.

A daily routine can run almost unnoticed. Coffee before anything. The same podcast on the drive. Checking the locks at night. Small repeated things hold a day together, like the hinges on a door. Sikhs have a routine like this too, but it's made of words. At dawn, at dusk and at night, many Sikhs recite set hymns from the Gurus. Not new words each day. The same words, day after day, for years, until they're part of the person.
screen: `COFFEE, PODCAST, LOCKS.` → `A ROUTINE MADE OF WORDS.` → `DAWN, DUSK AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The routine is called Nitnem. Nit means daily, always. Nem means a rule, a discipline, a vow you keep. So Nitnem is the daily discipline: a set of banis, hymns from the Gurus, said at fixed times. Bani simply means the word, the Guru's utterance. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, lays out three times. Morning: Japji Sahib, by Guru Nanak, then Jaap Sahib and the ten Savaiyas, by Guru Gobind Singh. Many Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five banis in the morning, adding Chaupai Sahib and Anand Sahib. Evening, at sunset: Rehras Sahib. Night, before sleep: Kirtan Sohila, which you met on day one hundred thirteen. Three doors in the day, each opened with the Guru's words. Some Sikh traditions and jathas include a few more banis or slightly longer versions; that comes later. Why the same words every day? Walk across a field once and it's just grass. Walk it every day and it becomes a path, and your feet find it in the dark. Daily banis can work like that on the mind. Over years, the lines surface on their own: in traffic, at a hospital bed, at a wedding. And Nitnem isn't only for the devout few. Children learn it at home, grandparents keep it, and many Sikhs listen along to a recording on the way to work. In the coming days, each bani gets its own day, plainly, one at a time.
screen: `NIT — DAILY. NEM — A DISCIPLINE.` · `MORNING: JAPJI, JAAP, SAVAIYAS.` · `EVENING REHRAS, NIGHT SOHILA.` · `A PATH WORN INTO THE FIELD.` · then, large: `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture your morning, right after you wake: that's the first door. Then your evening, as the light goes and work ends, the second, and the moment before sleep, lights off, the third. Walk through them slowly, morning, evening, night, without filling them with anything yet; just notice each one is there.
Nitnem. The daily discipline: set banis of the Gurus said at dawn, at dusk and at night.
Your line: morning, evening, night. Three doors in every day, each with its own words. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Nitnem daily: Japji, Jaap and the Savaiyas (and often Chaupai and Anand) in the morning, Rehras Sahib at sunset and Kirtan Sohila before sleep, from memory, from a gutka or along with a recording.

fork.setup: it's sunset and the day's work is done. which bani do many Sikhs turn to now?
fork.reveal: Rehras Sahib is the evening bani. Japji belongs to the morning, and Kirtan Sohila to the moment before sleep.

trapdoor: what you thought: a daily prayer.
what it means: a set of the Gurus' banis said at dawn, at dusk and at night, the same words for a lifetime.
what a scholar hears: nem is usually linked to the Sanskrit niyama, a vowed observance; the Rehat Maryada fixes the banis for each time.

notes: The Rehat Maryada's list: morning Japji, Jaap, Ten Savaiyas; evening Rehras; night Sohila. Many Amritdhari Sikhs recite five morning banis (adding Chaupai and Anand). Confirm how the Keeper wants the three-versus-five framing.
'Some jathas include more banis or longer versions' (e.g., Damdami Taksal's longer Rehras) is left general; day 136 returns to it.
Nem from Sanskrit niyama: common etymology. Confirm.
